# Summary

Permutation tests compare a result from the observed data with results calculated after rearranging the data. Which rearrangements are valid under the null hypothesis depends on how the data were collected. For example, freely shuffling a time series would destroy its ordering. `permute` is an R package for specifying these restrictions and generating permutations that follow them [@permute2026].

The package draws on designs introduced by Cajo J. F. ter Braak in CANOCO 3.1 and refined in later versions [@terBraak1990; @terBraakSmilauer2012]. It supports free permutations, cyclic shifts for series and transects, toroidal shifts that wrap around rectangular grids, and designs with blocks, plots, or subplots. Users can generate a single permutation, a random set, or all possible permutations. The same design can be used in different statistical procedures.

# Statement of need

A permutation test relies on exchangeability under the null hypothesis. This means that the joint distribution of the data stays the same after any rearrangement allowed by the test [@lehmannRomano2005, sec. 15.2; @hemerikGoeman2018]. When observations can be shuffled freely, `sample()` may suffice. Repeated measurements may need to stay with their site, a transect may require shifts that preserve order, and a spatial grid may require shifts that keep neighbours together. In a split-plot design, whole plots and subplots may be rearranged at different levels.

Implementing the same restrictions in several analysis functions makes them harder to test and can lead to inconsistent results. `permute` lets analysts specify and check the rules for rearranging their data, then reuse those rules across analyses. With few required dependencies, `permute` gives other R packages a simple way to generate permutations for the models they already use.

# State of the field

CANOCO is a package for multivariate analysis, including ordination and regression. Developed in the 1980s, it is widely used in ecology and environmental science. CANOCO made several permutation schemes available for ecological ordination, including cyclic shifts for time series and transects, toroidal shifts for rectangular grids, and restrictions for blocked and split-plot designs [@terBraak1990; @terBraak1992; @terBraakSmilauer2012]. `permute` implements these schemes in R. The cyclic and toroidal shifts are related to the work on spatial Monte Carlo tests discussed by @besagClifford1989.

R packages use permutations for different purposes (@tbl-package-comparison). Some implement particular tests. `coin` provides conditional tests of independence [@hothorn2008coin], `exactRankTests` provides exact rank and permutation tests [@exactRankTests], and `flip` provides multivariate permutation and rotation tests [@flip]. `lmPerm` focuses on linear models [@lmPerm], while `permuco` covers regression, repeated-measures ANOVA and ANCOVA, and signal comparisons [@frossardRenaud2021].

Combinatorics packages focus on mathematical arrangements. `arrangements`, `RcppAlgos`, and `gtools` generate permutations and combinations [@arrangements; @RcppAlgos; @gtools]. `partitions` handles integer and set partitions [@hankin2006; @hankinWest2007], and `permutations` works with algebraic permutations [@hankin2020]. `randomizeR` generates treatment assignments and evaluates allocation rules for clinical trials [@uschner2018]. `vegan` uses permutation designs in ecological analyses [@vegan].

| Category | Examples | Purpose | Restrictions and statistics |
|---|---|---|---|
| \rowcolor{permuteStripe} Statistical tests | `coin`, `permuco`, `flip` | Run specific tests | Restrictions and statistic depend on the test |
| Combinatorics | `arrangements`, `RcppAlgos` | Enumerate mathematical arrangements | No exchangeability design or statistic |
| \rowcolor{permuteStripe} Trial allocation | `randomizeR` | Generate treatment sequences | Allocation rules and assessment tools |
| Analysis | `vegan` | Analyse ecological data | Uses `permute` designs and supplies test statistics |
| \rowcolor{permuteStripe} Permutation design | `permute` | Generate permitted rearrangements | Series, grids, and nested designs. Users choose the statistic. |

Table: Roles of selected R packages related to permutations. {#tbl-package-comparison tbl-colwidths="[23,16,28,33]"}

`permute` defines which rearrangements are allowed so that the same design can be used with different test statistics.

# Software design

A `permute` design can describe blocks, plots, and observations within plots. @tbl-permutation-designs summarises the available schemes and restrictions.

Blocks are the outermost groups, and observations stay in their original block. Whole plots can be rearranged within blocks. `Plots()` sets the rules for rearranging plots, and `Within()` sets the rules for rearranging observations within plots. With no plots, `Within()` applies within blocks or across the whole data set if there are no blocks. `how()` combines these settings. You can supply the groups for blocks and plots directly or specify them with formulas.

In the following design, sites stay within their blocks and observations stay within their sites. Within each block, the same cyclic time shift is applied to the observations at every site. `shuffleSet()` returns a matrix of permutation indices that can be reused.

::: {#tbl-permutation-designs .sideways-table}

```{=latex}
\begin{tabular}{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.18}}

\toprule
Concept & What changes & What is preserved or required & Control \\
\midrule
\rowcolor{permuteStripe} Free permutation & Samples or whole plots are reordered freely within their group. & Group membership stays fixed. & \texttt{type = "free"} in \texttt{Within()} or \texttt{Plots()} \\
Cyclic shift & Samples or whole plots shift along a series or transect with wraparound. & Members of the circular sequence keep the same neighbours. Optional reflection reverses the order. & \texttt{type = "series"} in \texttt{Within()} or \texttt{Plots()} \\
\rowcolor{permuteStripe} Toroidal shift & Samples or whole plots shift along both axes of a rectangular grid with wraparound. & Samples or plots keep the same neighbours under wraparound. Optional reflection can be limited to one axis per permutation. & \texttt{type = "grid"} in \texttt{Within()} or \texttt{Plots()} \\
Fixed-size group assignment & Individual samples are reassigned to labelled groups. & Each group retains its original sample count. & \texttt{Plots(type = "partition")} \\
\rowcolor{permuteStripe} Whole-plot predictor assignment & Plot-level predictors, such as treatment labels, are reassigned jointly among plots. & Predictors must be constant within each plot. Samples and responses stay fixed. Sample counts may differ among plots. & \texttt{Plots(type = "free", variables = \textasciitilde{} treatment)} \\
Blocking & Permutations take place separately within each block. & Block membership stays fixed. & \texttt{how(blocks = \textasciitilde{} block\_id)} \\
\rowcolor{permuteStripe} Whole-plot rearrangement & Whole plots move with their samples. & Sample counts must match among plots within each block, or across all plots in an unblocked design. & \texttt{Plots()} with \texttt{"free"}, \texttt{"series"}, or \texttt{"grid"} \\
Split-plot permutation & Whole plots and the samples within them can be rearranged at their respective levels. & Samples stay with their original plot. When whole plots are rearranged, sample counts must match within each block, or across all plots in an unblocked design. & Combine \texttt{Plots()} and \texttt{Within()} in \texttt{how()} \\
\rowcolor{permuteStripe} Fixed ordering at one level & Permutations can proceed at the other level. & The chosen level retains its original ordering. & \texttt{type = "none"} in \texttt{Plots()} or \texttt{Within()} \\
Common within-plot permutation & The same rearrangement is applied within each plot in a block. & Plots must have equal sample counts. & \texttt{Within(constant = TRUE)} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
```

Permutation design concepts in `permute` 0.10-1.

:::

```{=latex}
\clearpage
```

```{r}
#| label: cyclic-time-shifts
#| message: false
library("permute")

dat <- data.frame(
  block = gl(4, 12),
  site = gl(8, 6)
)
ctrl <- how(
  plots = Plots(strata = ~ site, type = "none"),
  within = Within(type = "series", constant = TRUE),
  blocks = ~ block,
  nperm = 999,
  data = dat
)
set.seed(20112026)
perms <- shuffleSet(nrow(dat), control = ctrl)
```

`check()` checks a design against the data. `numPerms()` counts possible permutations and `allPerms()` lists small sets. For observations, `shuffle()` returns one ordering and `shuffleSet()` one per matrix row. Reuse the matrix across test statistics or parallel workers.

`permutations()` reorders a vector. `permutator()` steps through a supplied or generated set. Save the design settings and R's random seed to reproduce the permutations.

# Worked example

R's `CO2` data record carbon dioxide uptake at seven ambient concentrations in twelve *Echinochloa crus-galli* plants from Quebec and Mississippi [@potvin1990]. Half the plants from each location underwent daytime chilling, then overnight recovery. We test for a chilling effect by shuffling whole plants within location blocks (`Type`), keeping their measurements together.

```{r}
#| label: co2-design
data("CO2", package = "datasets")
co2 <- as.data.frame(CO2)

ctrl <- how(
  blocks = ~ Type,
  plots = Plots(strata = ~ Plant, type = "free"),
  within = Within(type = "none"),
  nperm = 9999,
  data = co2
)
```

This gives `{r} ctrl |> getBlocks() |> nlevels()` blocks and `{r} ctrl |> getPlots() |> getStrata() |> nlevels()` plots.

```{r}
#| label: co2-design-blocks-plants
ctrl |> getBlocks() |> nlevels()
ctrl |> getPlots() |> getStrata() |> nlevels()
```

The test statistic is the difference in mean uptake between treatments across concentrations. `permutations()` applies the design, returning one row of shuffled uptake values per permutation.

```{r}
#| label: co2-test
effect <- function(y) {
  with(co2,
    mean(y[Treatment == "chilled"]) - mean(y[Treatment == "nonchilled"])
  )
}

set.seed(20261120)
uptake <- permutations(co2$uptake, control = ctrl)
observed <- effect(co2$uptake)
null <- apply(uptake, 1, effect)
p_value <- (sum(abs(null) >= abs(observed)) + 1) / (length(null) + 1)

# show observed difference of means and permutation p value
observed |> round(4)
p_value |> round(4)
```

The mean difference was about `{r} observed |> round(2)` μmol m^-2^ s^-1^ (two-sided Monte Carlo *p* = `{r} p_value |> round(4)`).

# Research impact statement

`permute` began in `vegan` and became a separate package so other projects could reuse its code. It has been developed openly for over fifteen years and available on CRAN since 2011. On 20 November 2026, the source indexes listed 25 CRAN packages that depend on or import `permute` and four Bioconductor packages that import it. These include `vegan`, `permuco`, `randomizationInference`, `indicspecies`, and `codyn`, which support community ecology, experimental analysis, randomisation inference, indicator-species analysis, and temporal diversity research.

On the same date, Google Scholar listed 415 direct citations. CRAN Logs recorded about 6.9 million downloads from the RStudio CRAN mirror between 1 October 2012 and 20 November 2026. Many likely came via `vegan`, which requires `permute`.

`vegan` uses `permute` to set up permutations for ordination and other ecological tests. Other packages can accept a design from `how()` or an existing matrix of permutations. This lets users specify the rules once and reuse the same set of permutations across analyses.
